abstract: Quiescence is a reversible, non-proliferative cellular state in which cells can remain for extended periods of time while retaining the ability to re-enter the cell cycle upon exposure to favorable conditions. This physiological state is critical for a broad range of biological processes, from stress response in unicellular systems to differentiation and development in multicellular organisms. Surprisingly, despite its recognized roles in cell biology in diverse species, key aspects of the regulation of quiescence remain poorly understood. To investigate protein function specifically in quiescence, a conditional activation approach is critical, in particular for factors that are essential for cell viability. However, the efficacy of a number of such inactivation strategies in quiescent cells remained unknown. Using nitrogen-depleted fission yeast cells as a well-established model for quiescence, we probed two types of commonly-used approaches: a targeted method for the reversible inhibition of engineered kinases using non-hydrolyzable ATP analogs, and a more general system targeting protein depletion using an auxin-inducible degron. Here we show that the use of analog-sensitive kinases is unsuitable for quiescent fission yeast cells, as the ATP analog serves as a nitrogen source and induces cell cycle re-entry. We then demonstrate how coupling a degron tag with a specific auxin ligand allows for rapid, lasting and reversible protein depletion in quiescent cells, providing a powerful tool for investigating the regulation of this crucial and widespread cellular state.
